title: When a working system fails
kicker: Availability is more than a running process
heading: Restarting a container is not the same as recovering a service.
summary: Revisit the API, Valkey, and Postgres-QL system. Distinguish replacement of disposable compute from continuity of client work and durable records.
question: If an API Pod disappears, which parts of the system can actually recover?
explore: Sketch three failure consequences: an interrupted request, a replacement Pod, and an unavailable datastore.
observe: The Pod controller may restore the desired replica count, but application success and data safety require separate evidence.
confusion: All Pods show Ready. Does that prove the application recovered?
recover: Compare requests and database behavior from the client perspective. Ready is one signal, not a complete recovery test.

title: What survives a replacement?
heading: Every layer has its own lifecycle.
summary: Inspect the container filesystem, Pod lifetime, runtime configuration, and persistent data before replacing an API instance.
question: What state disappears with a Pod—and what should survive?
explore: Before removing anything, identify which values come from the image, environment, process memory, and persistent storage.
observe: Replacement restores code and configuration, but not arbitrary writes in a disposable container layer.
confusion: The Pod returned to Running; I expected all state to return too.
recover: Separate memory, writable layers, ephemeral volumes, and PersistentVolumeClaims. Compare where the record was stored.

title: Give data a lifecycle of its own
heading: A persistent claim decouples storage from Pod replacement.
summary: Explore PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, StorageClasses, and StatefulSets. In a local kind cluster, persistent storage is not equivalent to node-level high availability.
question: If the database Pod moves, where is its data actually stored?
explore: Trace the relationship: database container → mounted volume → claim → volume → underlying storage.
observe: A claim may be rebound to a replacement workload, but local storage remains vulnerable to loss of its backing node.
confusion: A bound PersistentVolumeClaim means the data is highly available.
recover: Inspect the StorageClass, provisioner, access mode, reclaim policy, and physical backing. Bound is not the same as redundant.

title: Persistence is not a backup
heading: A backup becomes credible when you successfully restore it.
summary: Use logical Postgres-QL backup concepts to define an independent restore test, then contrast persistence with recovery point and recovery time objectives.
question: What evidence shows that the backup can restore useful data?
explore: Design a disposable target database and a known record-count check. Predict what a backup cannot undo about a subsequent bad write.
observe: Restored data is independently queryable and meets an explicitly stated expected result.
confusion: A dump file exists; should I call the backup successful?
recover: Treat a file as unverified until it is restored to a separate environment and inspected. Check dump format and tool compatibility.

title: Healthy, ready and alive
heading: A running process may be unable to serve a request.
summary: Compare how readiness changes traffic eligibility, liveness can trigger a restart, and startup gates initial checks. Avoid turning temporary dependency outages into restart storms.
question: When should Kubernetes remove a Pod from traffic instead of restarting it?
explore: Predict behavior for three conditions: slow startup, temporary database failure, and unrecoverable deadlock.
observe: Probe outcomes lead to different actions. Readiness failure and liveness failure are not interchangeable.
confusion: A readiness failure restarts the container.
recover: Readiness does not, by itself, restart the container. Examine probe type, events, and configured thresholds.

title: Give requests time to finish
heading: Planned termination should not behave like a surprise crash.
summary: Inspect termination signals, grace periods, in-flight requests, and asynchronous removal of terminating endpoints. Avoid promising that all client requests will always succeed.
question: What happens to a request that is in flight when its Pod begins terminating?
explore: Compare a short request, a long-running request, and an abrupt kill. Predict which ones can finish in the grace period.
observe: SIGTERM handling, grace period, and endpoint removal coordinate imperfectly; existing connections may still need to finish.
confusion: When a Pod is Terminating, no client can still reach it.
recover: Consider open connections and delayed convergence; inspect endpoint conditions and app signal handling.

title: Deploy without creating an incident
heading: A successful rollout is verified from client behavior.
summary: Observe maxSurge, maxUnavailable, readiness gating, and Deployment revisions. Distinguish reverting an application from reversing database changes.
question: How can a new release fail without taking the whole Service down?
explore: Predict the rollout when new Pods stay unready. Observe the relationship between desired replicas, available replicas, and revision history.
observe: New Pods gain eligibility only after readiness succeeds; rollback requires behavioral verification.
confusion: A successful rollout undo also restores old database contents.
recover: Rollbacks change the Deployment Pod template; they do not automatically reverse schema migrations or restore deleted data.

title: Break it deliberately
heading: Predict → Disrupt → Observe → Recover → Verify.
summary: Introduce a known fault only in the disposable learning cluster; compare Kubernetes state with actual client outcomes and declare the limits of single-node kind.
question: What failure would best reveal a weakness in the system?
explore: Choose a fault and a prediction, then list evidence from the client, controller, and datastore points of view.
observe: A causal explanation: which condition changed, how it was detected, and how recovery was independently verified.
confusion: Deleting a Pod proves that the cluster is highly available.
recover: A single-node cluster can show controller-level recovery, but cannot prove node or storage high availability.

title: Checkpoint 3: Prove recovery
heading: Document what survived, what failed, and what recovered.
summary: Consolidate persistent-record checks, isolated restore evidence, readiness observations, graceful-termination behavior, and one faulty rollout or Pod failure.
question: Could another engineer reproduce your failure and verify the recovery?
explore: Assemble five artifacts: failure hypothesis, baseline, observation, recovery action, and independent functional verification.
observe: An evidence-backed claim that identifies exactly which failure modes the lab did—and did not—test.
confusion: The replicas are Ready, so I can mark Checkpoint 3 complete.
recover: Add a client-side functional test, the restored record validation, and precise limits of the local cluster.
